exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with painless hematuria; what epithelial change explains his risk for bladder cancer — transitional epithelium metaplasia due to Schistosoma haematobium.
A child with chronic diarrhoea shows villous atrophy on biopsy; which epithelial type is primarily affected and why — simple columnar absorptive cells lose microvilli, reducing nutrient uptake.

You see a thickened, scaly plaque on a HIV‑positive patient’s palm; which epithelial layer is involved and what is the most likely diagnosis — stratified squamous epithelium; likely eczema or fungal infection, differentiate by KOH prep.

During a ward round you note a patient with a non‑healing ulcer on the leg; what key histological feature would confirm squamous cell carcinoma — invasive nests of atypical squamous cells breaching the basement membrane.

A patient with long‑standing schistosomiasis develops dysuria; which investigation is most feasible in a low‑resource setting and what result would you expect — urine microscopy; detection of Schistosoma eggs.

In a malaria‑endemic area a newborn has a moist, red perineal rash; which epithelial type is involved and what supportive care is essential — stratified squamous epithelium; keep area dry and treat secondary infection.
You are asked to differentiate between simple and stratified epithelium on a biopsy; what histological clue is decisive — number of cell layers; simple has one layer, stratified has multiple.

A patient on chronic steroids develops oral thrush; why is the mucosal epithelium vulnerable — immunosuppression reduces local immunity, allowing Candida overgrowth on pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
ai.title: Epithelial Tissue
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Epithelial tissue lines body surfaces and cavities, providing protection, secretion, absorption and sensation. Recognising its types helps diagnose skin lesions, mucosal infections and cancers, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Classified by cell layers (simple vs stratified) and shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).
Specialised forms include ciliated, glandular and transitional epithelium.
sections.p: Epithelial tissue forms continuous sheets covering external and internal surfaces. Cells are tightly joined, rest on a basement membrane, and lack extensive blood vessels.
Understanding epithelial structure predicts function and common pathologies.

b: Schistosoma haematobium causes bladder transitional epithelium metaplasia → squamous cell carcinoma.
Chronic fungal or bacterial skin infections exploit compromised stratified squamous epithelium.
Malnutrition and HIV increase risk of oral candidiasis on mucosal epithelium.
sections.p: Damage or transformation of epithelium underlies many tropical and low‑resource conditions.

t.b: Identify fungal or bacterial organisms when culture unavailable; a positive KOH prep confirms candidiasis.
Detect hematuria or schistosome eggs; presence of eggs indicates urinary schistosomiasis.

t.a: Fine‑needle aspiration of a suspicious lesion
t.b: Distinguish benign hyperplasia from carcinoma when histology services are limited.

b: Simple columnar with microvilli → site of nutrient absorption; loss suggests villous atrophy in tropical sprue.
Ciliated pseudostratified columnar → common site for TB or chronic bronchitis; look for sputum production.
Transitional epithelium → bladder cancer risk in schistosomiasis endemic areas.
sections.p: Exam questions often link epithelial type to disease patterns.

b: Calling stratified cuboidal epithelium ‘simple’; it is multilayered and found in ducts.
Assuming all skin lesions are infectious; many are neoplastic arising from epithelial dysplasia.
Ignoring that epithelial tumours spread by local invasion before metastasis.
sections.p: Students frequently confuse epithelial classifications or overlook the basement membrane’s role.
